claims.text: Short-range ordering and clustering of like atomic pairs govern the mechanical behavior of initially undeformed refractory high-entropy alloys.
Short-range ordering and clustering of like atomic pairs govern the thermoelastic behavior of initially undeformed refractory high-entropy alloys.
Electronic-structure-based linear-response calculations drive the formation of short-range ordering and clustering.
Atomistic rearrangements at high strain promote changes in chemical clustering.
Molecular-dynamics simulations can characterize high-temperature short-range ordering, pair probabilities, and structural properties in high-entropy alloys.
High-entropy alloys can exhibit substantial chemical clustering over a broad temperature range.
Short-range ordering and like-pair clustering improve the mechanical strength of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Short-range ordering and like-pair clustering improve the thermoelastic behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Refractory high-entropy alloys can provide high-temperature mechanical performance superior to conventional nickel-based superalloys.
The proposed explanation applies to high-temperature service above 1000 degrees Celsius.
Impurities can alter the microstructure and mechanical behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys during thermal aging.
The exact role of impurities in the proposed ordering-based mechanism remains unclear.
The effect of phase separation on deformation behavior remains unclear.
A controlled comparison between otherwise equivalent refractory high-entropy alloys with and without short-range ordering and like-pair clustering can isolate the effect of that structural state.
If strength and thermoelastic behavior are comparable in samples with and without short-range ordering and like-pair clustering, the proposed causal role of ordering is falsified.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is scoped to an initial, undeformed state, but its proposed atomistic mechanism requires high-strain rearrangements; it does not explain how a high-strain process governs the stated undeformed state.

The stated intervention is molecular-dynamics simulation, whereas the falsification design calls for a controlled comparison of alloys with and without ordering. The hypothesis does not specify whether this comparison is computational or experimental or how ordering would be independently controlled.
